title: TB5-04492
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection. She has not submitted new evidence in support of her claim and she has not requested an oral hearing. The Appellant requests that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the determination of the RPD and find the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Alternatively, the Appellant requests that the RAD remit the matter to the RPD for reconsideration by a differently-constituted panel. Determination

Pursuant to section 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes a finding that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. The appeal is allowed. Background

The Appellant alleged she is a devout Ahmadi and that she and her family have been harassed, discriminated against and persecuted over their lifetime because of their religion. She further alleged there has been an upsurge in anti-Ahmadi activities since 2008 and since the bombing of Ahmadi mosques in Lahore in 2010. She has not been able to offer Friday prayers at the mosque. The issues
The panel indicated the determinative issues in regard to this claim are credibility, objective fear, subjective fear and internal flight alternative (IFA).

The Appellant submits the issues in this case are the following: What is the applicable standard of review? Did the RPD err in law by failing to conduct a section 97 analysis? Did the RPD err in finding that the Appellant has viable IFAs in Gujrat, Sargodha and Mandi Bahauddin? Did the RPD err in finding that the Appellant can freely practice her religion in Pakistan? Did the RPD err in finding that the Appellant lacks a subjective fear of persecution? Did the RPD make unsustainable credibility findings? Did the RPD err in finding that the Appellant's fear has no objective basis? The role of the RAD
While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.
The RAD now has the benefit of Federal Court jurisprudence which speaks to the appellate tribunal's role in relation to that of the RPD.

In this regard, the Court in Huruglica considered the appropriate relationship between the RAD and the RPD.1 In Huruglica, the Court determined that the RAD is to conduct a "hybrid appeal". It is to review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of the Appellant's refugee claim, deferring to the RPD only where the lower tribunal enjoys a particular advantage in reaching a conclusion. Where the RAD's assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own determination.

The Court determined that, in conducting its assessment, the RAD can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion. The RAD is, however, not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on the facts only where there is "palpable and overriding error."
The RAD will review all of the evidence in the RPD record and come to its own independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

The Appellant provides a brief analysis concerning the appropriate standard of review in this case, including an argument that the RAD owes no deference to the findings of the RPD. The RAD has provided above its view of its role in this case, including an indication where deference to the RPD findings is appropriate. Objective Fear

The panel noted the Appellant testified regarding her fear of extremists who threatened her family over the years because they were Ahmadis. The Appellant referred to incidents with neighbours and the panel found such acts of aggression deplorable but they did not amount to persecution.

The panel noted the Appellant and her family lived in the same house XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The panel noted it was reasonable to assume that the family's ability to secure a home from her husband's employer was not constrained by their Ahmadi faith.

The Appellant testified her husband retired in 1996 and they constructed a new home in another area of Lahore. The Appellant testified that neighbours harassed them, they were verbally abused and rocks were thrown at their home. The Appellant lived there from 1996 to 2014 when she came to Canada and her husband still lives there.

The panel noted the Appellant was vague regarding the last time she was harassed and that she recalled no specific incident that would amount to persecution. The panel found the Appellant's evidence lacked credibility and that the incidents of continuing harassment described by the Appellant were embellished to establish her claim.

The panel acknowledged the Appellant's contention that Ahmadis in Pakistan are subject to serious discrimination "if not in some instances persecution" by the State and non-State agents. The panel cited documentation concerning legislation that restricts the ability of Ahmadis to practice their faith and possible sanctions such as fines and imprisonment. The panel noted as well if blasphemy is found, there is a risk of the death penalty although this penalty has not been carried out. The panel further acknowledged that in the context of this legislation, Ahmadis are subject to attacks by non-state actors.

The Appellant testified that she is afraid to discuss her religion with non-Ahmadis because it is against the law. The panel noted the Appellant mentioned in her Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative, Ordinance 20 enacted in 1984 which constrains Ahmadis from discussing their religion with others but she did not mention any grievances in this regard. The panel further noted there was no evidence that the Appellant ever experienced difficulties in this regard or ever had any desire to proselytize and discuss her faith with non-Ahmadis. The panel found it was reasonable to determine in this context that there was less than a mere possibility of persecution from state agents if the Appellant were to return to Pakistan and practice her faith as she did in the past.

The panel noted that the constraint on Ahmadi women attending a mosque was made by the Ahmadi Jamaat in response to the attacks on Ahmadi mosques in Lahore in 2010. The panel further noted there is no evidence that women were particular targets of the attacks or that the Appellant was a particular target. The panel noted as well there was no evidence that the Appellant, if she returned to Pakistan, could not offer prayers in the same manner available to other Ahmadi women.

The panel acknowledged that documentary evidence provided by the Appellant and in the National Documentation Package supports the Appellant's contention some members of religious minorities, including Ahmadis, are subject to societal abuses, discrimination, and/or persecution at the hands of extremists and/or the authorities.2

The panel cited country document evidence indicating that in recent years scores of Ahmadis have been murdered in attacks that appear to be religiously motivated. The document further states that there is a climate of impunity where perpetrators feel empowered to attack Ahmadis without fear of arrest or prosecution. The panel notes, however, that the incidence of attacks by extremists is less than one half of one percent and the Appellant lacks the profile of those specifically targeted.
The panel acknowledged that the Appellant would have suffered discrimination, but noted there is nothing in the evidence that these acts of discrimination amount to persecution Subjective Fear

The panel noted the Appellant made no attempt to leave Pakistan although she testified that she and her family experienced harassment and abuse from extremists over many years, and the conditions for Ahmadis worsened since the passage of Ordinance 20 in 1984. The panel further noted the Appellant was issued a passport in 2010, but she made no effort to leave Pakistan until after 2011 when her son and family came to Canada and made successful refugee claims. The panel drew a negative inference from the Appellant's not finding the means to leave Pakistan prior to 2014. The panel found the Appellant's total lack of effort goes directly to her lack of subjective fear. Internal Flight Alternative

The panel found that even allowing the Appellant would face more than a mere possibility of harm in Lahore, there is more than one viable IFA available to her. The panel further found that there is no serious possibility of persecution in Gujrat, Sargodha or Mandi Bahaudin, towns where she has a daughter residing with their families.

The panel cited the two-prong test as held in Rasaratnam and Thirunavukkarasu.3 The Appellant testified that she is unable to live in the same areas as her daughters because they have their own problems. The Appellant further testified that her sons-in-laws in Gujrat and Sargoda had to close their businesses because of anti-Ahmadi actions. The panel noted there was no evidence disclosed that the reason they closed their businesses had anything to do with their Ahmadi faith. The panel further stated that there was no evidence that the closure of these businesses would negatively affect the Appellant's ability to live in the same vicinity as her daughters.

The panel found that the kind of hardship the Appellant could face in regard to relocation to any of these proposed IFAs is that associated with relocation and not the kind of hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable. The Appellant's submissions and the RAD's analysis and decision

The Appellant submits the panel erred in law by failing to conduct a section 97 analysis. The Appellant further submits the panel found that she is a practising Ahmadi, that Ahmadis are subject to serious discrimination and persecution by state and non-state agents, that Pakistani laws restrict the free practice of the Ahmadi faith, that sanctions for those found in violation of these laws include fines, imprisonment and/or the death penalty, that this legislation is used by non-state actors to threaten and harass Ahmadis and Ahmadis are subject to attacks by non-state actors.

The Appellant cites Federal Court jurisprudence which holds that notwithstanding any credibility findings, the RPD must conduct a separate section 97 analysis where refugee claimants establish that they have a profile that may put them at risk.

The Appellant submits that the objective evidence clearly demonstrates that Ahmadis in Pakistan face a risk to their lives and a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment and that the situation for Ahmadis has become increasingly precarious. The Appellant further submits that the panel's legal error in failing to conduct a section 97 analysis is sufficient to warrant the RAD's intervention and that there is sufficient evidence for the RAD to set aside the panel's decision and find that the Appellant is a person in need of protection pursuant to section 97.

The RAD has reviewed and assessed all of the evidence in the RPD record including the documentary evidence cited by both the Appellant and the panel concerning the treatment of Ahmadis in Pakistan. The RAD notes in this regard that the panel acknowledged that the Appellant is a practising Ahmadi. The RAD further notes the panel cited evidence concerning the risks faced by Ahmadis in Pakistan.

The RAD finds that the evidence is clear that all Ahmadis face the risk of harassment, prejudice, abuse and violent actions from both the Pakistani State and non-state actors. The RAD further finds that as a result of anti-Ahmadi legislation, those who attack and harass Ahmadis are able to do so without the risk of sanctions by the authorities.

The RAD notes the panel acknowledges that scores of Ahmadis have been murdered in attacks that were likely religiously motivated, but the panel's response to this evidence is that less than one half of one percent of Ahmadis have been subject to physical harm. The RAD further notes the panel provides no evidentiary basis for its statistical based argument which led it to find that the Appellant faces less than a mere possibility of persecution if she were to return to Pakistan.

The RAD notes the panel found that the Appellant did not share her Ahmadis beliefs with non-Ahmadis and did not proselytize non-Ahmadis, and therefore she would be able to return to Pakistan and practice her religion as she had done in the past and there is less than a mere possibility that she would be at risk of persecution.

The RAD finds that it is beside the point as to whether the Appellant proselytized non-Ahmadis in Pakistan in the past and whether she would do so in the future. The documentary evidence, acknowledged by the panel, makes clear that all Ahmadis are at risk of harm in Pakistan whether they proselytize or not. It is clear as well from the documentary evidence, acknowledged by the panel, that all Ahmadis are denied religious freedom in Pakistan.

The RAD finds that documentary evidence cited above and reviewed by the RAD makes clear that all Ahmadis, including the Appellant, are at risk of harm in Pakistan and an assessment of this risk under section 97 is required. The RAD notes the panel made only a passing reference to section 97 in its concluding paragraph. This is an error in law and determinative. The RAD agrees with the Appellant in this regard.

The Appellant submits the panel erred in finding the Appellant had possible IFAs in Gujarat, Sargodha and Mandi Bahauddin. The Appellant further submits the panel ignored objective documentary evidence, which indicates there is no IFA for persecuted Ahmadis in Pakistan. The Appellant submits as well the panel provided no evidentiary basis to support its conclusion that these three towns are safer than any other city in Pakistan.

The Appellant cites country document evidence describing the persecution of Ahmadis in Pakistan and the risks they face throughout the country.4 The Appellant further cites documentary evidence that states that "no where, including Rabwah, [the home of a large Ahmadi population] is safe for Ahmadis as police refuse to give protection to an Ahmadi.5

In regard to the three proposed IFAs, the Appellant submits the panel erred in rejecting her evidence as to why she could not relocate to these towns. The Appellant notes, in addition to her son-in-law being forced to close his business in Gujrat, her daughter's children face problems and they have received death threats.

In regard to Sarghoda, the Appellant's son-in-law was forced to close his business and they fear for their children's safety as people have indicated their opposition to Ahmadis. In addition the panel failed to mention the Appellant's evidence that her son-law was killed and as indicated in the Appellant's BOC, the killer stated he committed this murder because the victim was Ahmadi. In regard to Mandi Bahaudin, the Appellant testified that her family members faced many problems because they are Ahmadis and an Ahmadi mosque in the district was bombed by extremists and eight people were killed.

The Appellant submits the panel did not take any issue with the credibility of these allegations but determined that an IFA was available to her in any of these towns. The Appellant notes that the panel indicated in its Reasons that there was no evidence that her sons-in-laws were required to closes their businesses because they were Ahmadis. The Appellant submits this finding was made in stark violation of the presumption of truthfulness.

The RAD has reviewed and assessed all of the evidence in the RPD record concerning the availability of an IFA for an Ahmadi in Pakistan. The RAD agrees with the Appellant that the panel has failed to provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for its finding that she has a safe haven available to her in any of the proposed IFAs. The RAD notes that other than the presence of a daughter in each of the three proposed IFAs, the panel provides no analysis as to why these three towns would allow the Appellant safety from harassment and abuse as opposed to a risk in Lahore or any other location in Pakistan. In addition, the RAD finds that the panel failed to provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for its challenge to the truthfulness of her evidence that her sons-in-laws were forced to close their businesses because they were Ahmadis.
The RAD concludes, on the basis of the totality of evidence available in the RPD record, that there is no IFA for the Appellant in Pakistan.

The Appellant submits that the panel erred in finding that she can freely practice her religion in Pakistan. The Appellant provides an extensive analysis of the test for religious persecution and acknowledges that there is no test that defines when interference with religious practices or proscription of one's religion amounts to persecution.

The RAD finds, in the context of the documentary evidence noted above and its assessment of all of the evidence in the RPD record that it is not possible for the Appellant, as an Ahmadi, to practice her religion freely in Pakistan. The RAD finds the panel's finding in this regard to be inexplicable and lacking a sufficient evidentiary basis. The RAD notes that the banning of proselytizing is only one of many Ahmadi beliefs and practices also banned by the Pakistan government. The RAD notes as well that this legislation has led to expanded anti-Ahmadi violence by non-state actors and the denial of state protection for Ahmadis by police authorities.

The RAD finds that if the Appellant were to return to Pakistan, there is a serious possibility that she would be at risk of harassment that cumulatively may rise to the level of persecution. The RAD further finds that the panel failed to consider the issue of cumulative persecution in response to the Appellant's evidence that she and her family experienced over time harassment, prejudice and abuse in her life in Pakistan because she is a practising Ahmadi. Disposition

Pursuant to section 111(1)(b) of IRPA, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and finds that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. The appeal is allowed.
